entries.title: Downtown and Near North Side District 6a Chicago School Board race too close to call
entries.summary:
District 6a neighborhoods: Near North Side, West Town

The candidate supported by a billionaire-backed political group and charter proponents continued to have a narrow lead over two progressives as of Thursday, but the race was too close to call.

With all precincts reporting, less than 1,000 votes separated Isaiah White, a school support worker; Anusha Thotakura, the incumbent who runs a statewide advocacy organization; and Brenda Lee Anderson, a Northwestern University lecturer on leave, according to Chicago Board of Election results.

Election officials have until Nov. 17 to finish counting mail-in ballots and provisional ballots. Final official results are due on Nov. 24.

White said his analysis showed that mail-in ballots historically haven't diverged more than 1% from the pattern of other ballots, which could keep him in the lead. "So, we are cautiously optimistic we will hold our lead, but not taking anything for granted," he said Thursday. "We are taking everything seriously."

The close race was somewhat unexpected. Voters in the area typically support more conservative candidates. But across the city, candidates supported by the Chicago Teachers Union are doing better than expected after being significantly outspent.

Thotakura got support from the CTU and the Service Employees International Union, which represents school support workers. She seems to be splitting the more left-leaning vote with Anderson, who was not backed by any special interests.

More than $500,000 was spent on White’s campaign by The Urban Center, a centrist political organization that advocates for school choice across public and private schools, and the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools. He also was endorsed by an anti-CTU political action committee that is heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and says it aims to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.”

Given its location as part of the commercial and business center of the city, District 6a has just 14 public schools — the fewest of any school board electoral districts — and none are neighborhood high schools. The students who attend Chicago Public Schools here include a more diverse mix than in most districts, but the schools have more white and Asian American students than CPS as a whole.

Two of the schools in the district have the highest rating given by the state; while 60% had the lowest two distinctions, “developing” and “comprehensive,” according to 2026 state data released last week. There are now six levels of designations, up from the five up last year when the bottom two were called “comprehensive” and “intensive.”

Thotakura’s and White’s main priorities are to boost reading and math scores. Anderson’s main goal is to fix CPS’ chronic budget crisis.

Contributing: Reema Amin, Chalkbeat Chicago and Kate Grossman

entries.title: Emma Lozano leads in District 7a Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 7a neighborhoods: South Lawndale, Near West Side, Lower West Side, Garfield Ridge, Archer Heights

Longtime Pilsen activist Emma Lozano was leading in this majority-Latino district as of Thursday, but the race remained too close to call.

Lozano had received just over 54% of the vote with ballots from five precincts still uncounted on Thursday, up from six unreported on election night, according to Chicago Board of Election results.

Election officials have until Nov. 17 to finish counting mail-in ballots and provisional ballots. Final official results are due on Nov. 24.

Lozano, first appointed in 2024 by Mayor Brandon Johnson, faced a challenge from Jesus Ayala Jr., a Chicago Public Schools graduate who worked for a nonprofit after-school program.

Lozano was endorsed by the Chicago Teachers Union, while Ayala had the backing of charter school advocates, groups that oppose the CTU and the Service Employees International Union Illinois State Council — which represents thousands of support staff in CPS and has split politically with the teachers union in recent years. Ayala tried to run in 2024, but his name was removed from the ballot after a successful challenge to the signatures on his nomination paperwork.

Ayala had raised $74,000 more than Lozano but she said the decades she spent advocating for education issues gave her the edge in the race.

“I think people remember that and that was able to carry me through,” Lozano said just after 10 p.m. Tuesday.

For Lozano, being part of Tuesday’s election felt like a revolutionary act, recalling a time when community members fought to get an elected school board. She was critical of how much money was poured into the various races.

Lozano will have to work with Jessica Biggs, who won the race for board president and was supported by groups who oppose the Chicago Teachers Union. Lozano said she would respect the election results but she won’t budge on her principles when it comes time to vote on matters before the board.

“There’s going to be some times, hopefully not just myself but others, will have to keep [Biggs] in her place,” Lozano said, adding that she wants to ensure resources are allocated to students living in mixed-status immigrant homes and providing better school lunches.

This Southwest Side district is home to 48 public schools. Last year, 64% received the state’s second-highest designation, “commendable,” while 4.5% received an “intensive” designation, indicating they remained among the bottom 5% of low-income schools in the state for four years after receiving comprehensive support or continued to have a graduation rate of 67% or below.

The students who attend District 7a schools are primarily Latino, matching the community demographics, and most come from families with low incomes. Nearly half are English learners.

Both Lozano and Ayala identified protecting immigrant communities and securing progressive revenue among their priorities.

entries.title: West Side District 5b Chicago School Board race too close to call
entries.summary:
District 5b neighborhoods: North Lawndale, Near West Side, East Garfield Park, West Garfield Park, West Town 

Michilla “Kyla” Blaise was leading in District 5b Thursday evening, but the school board race remained too close to declare a winner.

Blaise was holding the top spot with 52.5% of the votes, according to Chicago Board of Election results. By Thursday evening, all up but one voting precinct had reported results, up from four missing precincts early Wednesday morning.

Election officials have until Nov. 17 to finish counting mail-in ballots and provisional ballots. Final official results are due on Nov. 24.

Blaise, a political aide backed by the Chicago Teachers Union, was appointed by Mayor Brandon Johnson to the school board in 2024, and she was seeking a two-year seat on the school board representing a large swath of the West Side.

For challenger Anthony Hargrove, it was his second attempt at the seat after failing to make the ballot two years ago. Hargrove, who runs programs to help dropouts get back in school, had support from the Service Employees International Union Illinois State Council, which represents CPS support staff, charter school advocates like the Illinois Network of Charter Schools and the Common Ground Collective, an anti-CTU political action committee that’s heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks.

District 5b is one of the school board’s most economically diverse, stretching from the wealthy West Loop to historically disinvested neighborhoods such as North Lawndale and Garfield Park. It includes several neighborhood high schools struggling with declining enrollment, as well as some of CPS’ most in-demand magnet schools. Students who attend school here are mostly Black and Hispanic.

Students in District 5b are less likely to attend their neighborhood school than students in any other voting district in the city. Only 6% chose their local high school, while 35% chose their neighborhood elementary school.

The candidates homed in on different issues during the race. Blaise said she was focused on increasing funding for CPS, addressing declining enrollment and improving student mental health, while Hargrove zeroed in on improving reading and math proficiency, refining special education and expanding vocational and career education.

The two candidates aligned on some issues. They both support stronger restrictions on the use of artificial intelligence and cellphones in the classroom, and both oppose closing schools for any reason.

Notably, Blaise led the effort to pass a CPS budget that reversed some proposed cuts but banked on the state to provide $150 million in funding it had not committed. On his candidate questionnaire, Hargrove said the school board should continue to advocate for additional state funding and look for other savings “before cutting classroom programs or student services.”

Contributing: Mary Norkol

entries.title: Jason Dónes leads in District 3b Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 3b neighborhoods: Humboldt Park, Logan Square, Belmont Cragin, West Town, Hermosa

Incumbent Carlos Rivas Jr. and Jason Dónes remained neck and neck Thursday evening in their contest for a school board seat representing a district on the Near Northwest Side, according to Chicago Board of Election data.

All the precincts in the school board district were finally counted by Thursday evening and Rivas, a former-teacher-turned city communications director, trailed Jason Dónes by 180 votes. Until Thursday afternoon, four precincts had remained untabulated. With those additional precincts, Dónes' lead grew by 53 votes.

“We’re in the lead — we’re not chasing, but it is sight,” Dónes said Thursday midday as he took a break from work, which he described as a good distraction. “But call me in 30 minutes, and I might be down. Call again and I might be up … It’s a scary few days. Everyone is lighting a candle.”

Election officials have until Nov. 17 to finish counting mail-in ballots and provisional ballots. Final official results are to be released on Nov. 24.

It's a rematch for two men who both grew up in Humboldt Park, graduated from selective-enrollment Chicago public high schools, and became teachers through Teach for America. In 2024 Rivas Jr. won with 54% of the vote.

Both candidates identify as progressives. Rivas has taken a more fiscally conservative approach to the school budget than his opponent.

Bolstered by about $600,000 from groups that oppose the Chicago Teachers Union, Rivas also had support from the Service Employees International Union, which represents thousands of CPS school support staff and has split politically with the teachers union in recent years. Also behind him were charter school advocates, some Northwest Side officials and the the Common Ground Collective, a political action committee that opposes the CTU, is heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and says it aims to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.”

Jason Dónes was backed by the CTU and several Northwest Side elected officials.

A few days before the election, Rivas responded to the release of records that showed he was suspended from his job at a charter school in 2018 after he became intoxicated at a work event and engaged in “unwanted touching” of a co-worker.

Rivas said the incident happened at a difficult time in his life when he was caring for his dying mother and that he took responsibility for what happened and got help through an employee assistance program.

“I believe in accountability, growth and second chances,” he told the Chicago Sun-Times in a statement. Rivas worked as a teacher, college counselor and external affairs manager at the school. He is now the public affairs director for the Civilian Office of Police Accountability.

Schools in District 3b are struggling with teacher and counselor shortages, higher property taxes, and low enrollment amid rapid gentrification. The district includes a mix of 32 schools serving mostly Latino students. The schools are generally strong, with about 60% achieving the state’s second highest rating last year. But 6% have the lowest of the five ratings.

Rivas and Dónes both care about protecting immigrant students from federal immigration agents, supporting more affordable housing, and securing more resources and community partnerships for CPS families. Rivas says he wants less interference from the mayor on the board and to move away from using loans that will increase CPS’ budget deficit.

Dónes, a CPS parent, was looking to increase budget transparency, push for creative solutions within the existing budget framework, and said on our questionnaire that he wouldn’t accept contributions from corporations or “private interest groups funded by billionaires and millionaires.”

Rivas’ outside support was about five times greater than Dónes’. As of Monday, more than half of the $502,000 backing Rivas came from the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools while another $123,000 came from the anti-CTU Common Ground Collective. All of Dónes’ outside support comes from the CTU, totaling about $22,000.

Contributing: Ariel Parrella-Aureli of Block Club Chicago and Kate Grossman

entries.title: Election officials say coding error affected few precincts, but high voter turnout also led to long lines
entries.summary: <p>Chicagoans who voted on Election Day may have grown impatient in long lines, but only part of that can be attributed to a technical issue reported at some polling locations, the Chicago Board of Elections said. </p><p>A coding error the Chicago Board of Elections says is responsible for some polling places <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/04/election-coding-error-ballot-shortage" >receiving a low amount of ballots</a> affected less than 2% of precincts, but high voter registration and turnout contributed to long lines on Election Day, the Board of Elections said.</p><p>The board completed an audit Thursday that concluded the coding error miscalculated the number of ballot styles needed for some precincts only led to shortages at 24 precincts, or 1.86% of the board's total precincts. Board officials said its IT department has added validation checks and other precautions to hopefully identify and prevent similar issues in the future.</p><p>But high voter turnout and same-day voter registration rates also impacted lines on Election Day, the board said in a statement Thursday. More than 34,000 people registered to vote on Election Day and voter turnout was second only behind the 2024 presidential election. As a result, voting wait times and voter processing were slowed by those factors as well, the board said.</p>

entries.title: Fallece mujer que fue baleada en la cabeza mientras iba en auto en Brighton Park el mes pasado
entries.summary: <p>Una mujer de 32 años que fue baleada el mes pasado en el vecindario de Brighton Park, en lo que ha sido descrito como un episodio provocado por la ira vial, falleció hoy jueves en la mañana, según la policía.</p><p>Rosa D. Hernández Rivera, residente de Brighton Park, fue declarada muerta a las 5:17 a.m., según la policía y la Oficina del Médico Forense del Condado de Cook.</p><p>Hernández Rivera iba como pasajera en un vehículo en la cuadra 2400 al oeste de 47th Street alrededor de las 9:30 a.m. el 22 de octubre, cuando un auto gris se detuvo a su lado y alguien le disparó en la cabeza, dijo la policía.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7b0000" name="module-7b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El esposo de la mujer y dos de sus tres hijos también iban en el automóvil, según declaró al Chicago Sun-Times el concejal Raymond López (15.°) en ese entonces.</p><p>Después del tiroteo, el auto gris huyó hacia el sur por Western Avenue y Hernández Rivera fue llevada al Hospital Mount Sinai, inicialmente en estado crítico.</p><p>El esposo de Hernández Rivera había estado colaborando con la policía para identificar cámaras de vigilancia públicas y privadas en la zona que pudieran haber captado el incidente, dijo López en ese momento, y agregó que cree que la ira vial provocó el tiroteo.</p><p>Nadie más resultó herido.</p><p>Detectives del Área 1 investigan el caso.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Chicago voters overwhelmingly supported vacancy tax to help fund Chicago Public Schools
entries.summary: <p>Many Chicagoans consider the thousands of vacant lots scattered across the city to be an eyesore. And on Tuesday, a number of them said the lots should be a source of revenue for Chicago Public Schools.</p><p>Nearly 74% of Chicago voters were in favor of a referendum that would hit the owners of vacant or undeveloped property in the city with an annual tax that would support <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education" >CPS</a>. About 26%, or 163,655, of the city's 624,339 voters were against the idea.</p><p>The ballot question wasn't binding, meaning the tax won’t go into effect unless it’s introduced and then approved by the City Council. </p><p>CPS board members believe the results show there’s a will to make the vacant property tax a reality.</p><p>“We have a very divided City Council, but all of these people are up for election,” said Debby Pope, who retained her school board seat following Tuesday's closely watched <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-district-2b-results" >District 2b race</a>. “I imagine if [the referendum] got such a good mandate percentagewise … people who are running for election will have to take note.”</p><p>The referendum said the tax would be on “owners of long-term vacant or undeveloped commercial or investment properties,” but it didn’t specify what is considered long-term. It also didn't say a tax rate, making it unclear how much the so-called annual charge would amass for CPS, which faced a $730 million deficit entering this school year. The deficit would have been nearly $900 million if it hadn’t raised property taxes to the limit, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board/2026/10/13/cps-elected-school-board-budget-deficit-property-taxes-increase" >the Sun-Times previously reported</a>.</p><p>Taxes on vacant or blighted property aren’t new. Washington, D.C., implemented a <a class="Link" href="https://islg.cuny.edu/blog/vacant-property-taxes-to-spur-housing-development" target="_blank" >vacancy tax in 2011</a>, setting a higher tax rate for vacant and blighted properties. Baltimore approved a vacancy tax in 2024, which charges property owners three times their initial property tax rate the first year a building is deemed vacant and four times the tax rate each subsequent year. Baltimore’s vacancy tax went into effect July 1.</p><p>A spokesperson for Mayor Brandon Johnson said the administration understands concerns about underutilized properties and the importance of putting them back to productive use. They pointed to the mayor’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/04/03/chicago-missing-middle-program-families-south-west-sides-vacant-lot" >Missing Middle Infill Housing program</a>, which has created hundreds of new homes across the South and West sides by selling vacant lots to developers for $1.</p><p>“We believe vacant properties should be opportunities to strengthen our neighborhoods, create economic opportunity, and improve quality of life for residents,” the mayor’s office said in a statement. “We hear what Chicagoans are saying and remain committed to finding ways to put these properties to better use for the people of our city.”</p><p>Pope, a retired teacher, who was backed by the Chicago Teachers Union, said she saw firsthand how vacant lots near schools can become dumping grounds and a source of blight in communities. And a tax would stop vacant lots from becoming an eyesore — and a danger to neighbors, she said.</p><p>“It just disincentivizes people from holding on to them,” Pope said.</p><p>CPS board member Michilla Blaise, who’s leading the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-district-5b-results" >District 5b school board race</a>, said a vacancy tax would help solve two separate but related issues: the need for increased CPS revenue and the ability to position land for its highest and best economic value.</p><p>Although the proposal sounds great on paper, creating an actionable policy would be tricky and could slow future development.</p><p>Celadon Partners CEO Scott Henry said he understands CPS’ funding needs, but he thinks a vacancy tax isn't the right approach for both spurring development and supporting the school district.</p><p>“When I think about a vacant building or a vacant piece of land in Chicago, there's a really good reason why it's in that condition,” Henry said. “In a lot of situations, piling a fine on just makes a bad situation even worse. I don't know how collectible the fines would be. Implementing something like this just adds to the list as to why it's so difficult to do business in Chicago. We need to be creating programs or processes that create certainty and predictability if we're going to attract developers and investors back to the city.”</p><p>Henry said a feasible alternative would be allocating the city's tax increment financing to encourage developers to redevelop vacant properties. The city could then charge a one-time “impact fee” on developers — which could support CPS.</p><p>“It would be more predictable,” Henry said. “CPS probably would get a lot more revenue out of it, and at the end of it, we'd end up with a brand new redeveloped property that's generating revenue, providing quality housing and improving these neighborhoods.”</p>

entries.title: Illinois House Speaker Chris Welch says he'll step down as caucus leader in face of Democratic mutiny
entries.summary: <p>Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch announced Thursday he won't seek another term at the helm of his chamber next year, acknowledging his tenure was doomed after 26 Democratic state representatives signed a statement calling for a change in leadership.</p><p>The seismic statehouse shakeup comes in the wake of revelations over the summer that Welch was aware of sexual harassment allegations against disgraced ex-state Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield, almost three years before additional complaints prompted Benton’s resignation.</p><p>The call for new leadership was distributed late Wednesday by North Side state Rep. Kelly Cassidy, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/05/welch-benton-harassment-working-group-cassidy" target="_blank" ><u>the most vocal public critic</u></a> of Welch’s handling of the case and his formation of a working group that she dismissed as a "smokescreen” instead of addressing Springfield’s entrenched culture of harassment.</p><p>But the statement demanding Welch's ouster drew signatures from nearly a third of the caucus that’ll be sworn in with a new General Assembly in January, including Cicero state Rep. Lisa Hernandez, chair of the Democratic Party of Illinois. </p><p>“Over the course of the last few months, we have grown increasingly convinced that the House Democratic Caucus needs new leadership,” the lawmakers said. “We represent a broad spectrum of our caucus, and each have come to this decision for our own reasons. We look forward to a robust race for a new Speaker of the House.”</p><p>Within 16 hours of the public mutiny — and less than two days after an election that added even more seats to Democrats' supermajority caucus under a political operation spearheaded by Welch — he announced he'll step aside when a new General Assembly is sworn in in January.</p><p>“I am proud of this work, but I serve at the pleasure of the caucus, and I want our caucus to lead in unity and take on the mandate we received from voters this past election confidently,” Welch said in a statement. “With that, I look forward to joining the caucus as we usher in our next leader and take our party further into the future.”</p><p>Cassidy and three other Dems who led the push for change — state Reps. Mary Beth Canty of Arlington Heights, Tracy Katz Muhl of Northbrook and Larry Walsh of Elwood — later praised Welch for agreeing to give up the gavel.</p><p>“Speaker Welch has put the House Democratic Caucus before himself in his decision to clear the path for the emergence of new leadership," the representatives said in a statement. "We look forward to continuing to work with him as a fellow legislator.</p><p>"Because the Speaker made his announcement today, he has rightly afforded us plenty of time to ensure the process for choosing a new speaker is deliberate and intentional. We must ensure our next speaker is able to take the time necessary to earn the support of our caucus members, without interference or a finger on the scale from the current Speaker’s operation," they said. "New leadership must work thoughtfully and conscientiously to build a consensus for how we can best serve the needs of the people of Illinois.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-060000" name="image-060000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9e458c1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7122x3997+0+376/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F9d%2F90%2F9f54dbc04d9da45e24ca0c3d82e4%2Fimmigrantrights-110724-11.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3587162/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7122x3997+0+376/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F9d%2F90%2F9f54dbc04d9da45e24ca0c3d82e4%2Fimmigrantrights-110724-11.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ada6e6e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7122x3997+0+376/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F9d%2F90%2F9f54dbc04d9da45e24ca0c3d82e4%2Fimmigrantrights-110724-11.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="State Rep. Kelly Cassidy, D-Chicago, pictured at a Little Village news conference in 2024. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Post-election rebellion</h3><p>The revolt followed a historic flexing of political muscle by the three-term speaker’s campaign network, which expanded Democrats’ control of the House to a modern-record 78-40 supermajority in 2022.</p><p>The Welch-controlled Democrats for the Illinois House political committee raised $35 million <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/04/blue-tsunami-democrats-massive-advantage-illinois-general-assembly" target="_blank" ><u>to flip at least five more seats in Tuesday’s general election</u></a>, turning Illinois’ heavily gerrymandered political map an even deeper shade of blue. With two other seats still in play as mail ballots trickled in, that advantage could rise as high as 85-33 over Republicans.</p><p>“This is what a winning political operation looks like," Welch said in a statement the day after the election, several hours before the bloc of his colleagues called for a new speaker.</p><p>But the rebellion had been brewing behind the scenes for months since the Benton scandal broke also raised questions about Welch’s own behavior. His social media interactions with a complainant in the case left the young woman uncomfortable, for which he later apologized. </p><p>The list of his caucus defectors included three incoming representatives freshly elected with Welch’s backing, including state Rep.-elect Jessica Dixon Heitman, who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/us-illinois-house-97-midterm-results" >won a full term to Benton’s former seat</a> with the help of $1.6 million in support from Welch-controlled funds.</p><p>Nineteen of the 26 signatories are women. Four are part of Welch’s own leadership team: Hernandez, who’s deputy majority leader; plus assistant majority leaders Eva-Dina Delgado, Bob Morgan and Katie Stuart.</p><p>Absent Republican support, their votes would've been enough to block Welch from the gavel even if the rest of their party’s staggering new majority had stood by him.</p><h3>Democratic dissent</h3><p>Before Welch's announcement, Canty, the House Democratic Women’s Caucus chair, said she was confident more of her colleagues were ready for new leadership even if they weren't yet comfortable publicly defying Welch. </p><p>“The bigger concern is not that [Benton] scandal itself, but really the judgment it showed, from the way it was handled in ‘23, then to ‘26, and then the way it has been handled ever since it was first reported,” Canty said. “All of that shows a standard of judgment that hasn’t inspired confidence.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Several members passed on participating in the House working group Welch convened to discuss harassment reporting mechanisms in the Capitol.</p><p>Canty said she met with Welch over the summer, and "in that conversation it became clear for me that my concerns are solvable, but not solvable by this speaker," she said. </p><p>In a statement, state Rep. Anne Stava, D-Downers Grove, said "the decision came down to believing women who come forward as survivors of sexual harassment and creating a safer workplace environment for all who work in our Capitol and look to the Speaker for guidance and mentorship... Change is rarely easy, but in my experience worth the sacrifices needed to get there."</p><p>Stava suggested the new speaker should be a woman, which would be a first for the chamber. </p><p>Canty said “maybe now is the time we start looking to our female colleagues, but there are a lot of really great members in this caucus.”</p><p>“This is not about trying to pick someone new and put them immediately into the speaker’s role,” Canty said. “It’s important we have a process where candidates put their names forward, and then share with the caucus how they’ll run the chamber, how they’ll run the political operation, and take questions from our caucus.”</p><p>Cassidy — who said she’s “not even remotely” interested in becoming speaker — called the response to their rebellion “overwhelmingly positive.”</p><p>“I woke up to dozens of text messages from current and former [House] staffers thanking me,” she said. “The problems in our workplace are not limited to the House Democratic Caucus. Any solutions have to be done with both caucuses in both chambers. We need to do an honest accounting of what we haven’t done right.”</p><h3>Past concerns over Welch</h3><p>Welch finds himself forced out of the office for many of the same reasons it opened up for the first time in a generation about six years ago. </p><p>He was elected as Illinois’ first Black speaker in 2021 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/1/13/22228758/emanuel-chris-welch-illinois-house-speaker-vote-mike-madigan" target="_blank" ><u>in the wake of Michael Madigan’s downfall</u></a>, which was precipitated in part by the legendary ex-political boss’ mishandling of misconduct allegations within his once-vaunted 13th Ward organization. After Madigan’s 36 years as speaker, legislators set a limit of five terms with the gavel.</p><p>The Benton fiasco also renewed scrutiny of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/07/28/illinois-house-speaker-emanuel-chris-welch-harry-benton-michael-j-madigan-sexual-harassment-inquiry" target="_blank" ><u>a 2002 suburban police report</u></a> that alleged Welch slammed a woman’s head into a countertop during an argument. He was never criminally charged and has denied wrongdoing.</p><p>Cassidy, citing unresolved questions about that episode, was the lone Democrat not to support Welch’s initial ascent.</p><p>“I had my concerns in his first election as speaker because the issues had been raised,” she said. “I gave him the benefit of the doubt the second time around, but it's not acceptable after what we learned this summer.”</p><p>Even before the Benton scandal, some House Democrats had privately grumbled about Welch’s command of sometimes chaotic caucus meetings, as well as a policy of not calling bills for a floor vote without 60 Democrats first signaling support.</p><p>“I have worked tirelessly to serve this House Democratic Caucus," Welch said in his Thursday statement. "It is one that I love, and deeply respect. I have always told the caucus that our time in this space is finite, but we are playing an infinite game.</p><p>"Diversity is our strength, but unity is our power. Together, we passed historic legislation on transit, cannabis and energy, and secured greater investments in education. We defended vulnerable seats and grew our majority in every election under my leadership, building a historic House Democratic majority," Welch said. </p><p>The turnover adds a new layer of political uncertainty as lawmakers return to Springfield for the fall veto session Nov. 17, when Gov. JB Pritzker is hoping they'll to reach a compromise on legislation to help the Chicago Bears build a new stadium in Illinois. </p><p>A spokesperson for Pritzker didn't have any immediate comment. Earlier this week, the governor sidestepped questions about whether he thought Welch should stay in power. </p><p>"The members of the House get to choose who they want as a leader, and I look forward to working with whoever that may be... Right now, he's the speaker of the House, and I'll work with him."</p>

entries.title: Blackhawks doomed by Arvid Soderblom's soft goals allowed in latest loss
entries.summary: <p>TAMPA, Fla. — Many of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>' problems will require some big, difficult decisions by general manager Kyle Davidson to address.</p><p>One that wouldn't require shaking the earth, however, is changing the backup goalie.</p><p>Current backup Arvid Soderblom's struggles continued Thursday in a 4-1 loss to the Lightning, which extended the Hawks' losing streak to five consecutive games.</p><p>"There's probably a few [goals] there that he'd like to have back," coach Jeff Blashill conceded before saying the right things to take the heat off of Soderblom: "We're going to win or lose as a team. There's mistakes made throughout the game. [We've] got to stick together."</p><p>Davidson, who traveled with the Hawks for both games in Florida this week, surely has to be thinking long and hard about whether this team is capable of turning things around in its current form, even though their schedule does lighten considerably after this trip.</p><p>He also ought to be thinking long and hard about whether Soderblom can be a viable NHL goalie moving forward. Soderblom is now 0-3-1 with an .846 save percentage this season after going 8-13-3 with an .880 mark last season. </p><p>The Hawks have leaned heavily so far on starter Spencer Knight (13 starts in 17 games), but they have more back-to-back sets coming up that will need dividing.</p><p>The Lightning's first goal was a high-danger chance on a two-on-one rush, but Victor Hedman's not particularly well-aimed shot probably should've been stopped.</p><p>The Lightning's second and third goals, meanwhile, definitely should've been saved. They both beat Soderblom clean — one through the five-hole, one over the glove — from low-danger angles near the left circle.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Lightning goal: Ilya Mikheyev beats Soderblom to make it 2-0. <a href="https://t.co/XGc8rimiI0">pic.twitter.com/XGc8rimiI0</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2118504322765869264?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 6, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Hawks weren't the better team and didn't deserve a different outcome. They're generating painfully little offensively right now. Soderblom did make a few good saves, too, and has demonstrated an unflappable attitude.</p><p>The expected goals, however, were 2.79 to 2.14 (per Natural Stat Trick). That's a closer game than the 4-1 scoreline suggests, and goaltending is one reason for that disparity. That's a common theme in Soderblom starts throughout recent years, too.</p><p>Things aren't going any better for Rockford right now than they are for the Hawks, which means prospect goalie Drew Commesso has a lackluster .890 AHL save percentage beside his name. But a different look of any type seems worth a shot.</p><h3><b>Tampa trend</b></h3><p>The Hawks had bizarrely won each of the last three seasons in Tampa, with Ryan Donato's last-minute game-winning goal here last October marking arguably the high point of last season.</p><p>Donato admitted the Hawks' mood was "definitely different" after this result.</p><p>"But the effort’s there," Donato added. "The guys are working. We have a great group of guys...that love being with each other, want to compete and want to win. I think it’s a matter of time."</p><p>Ilya Mikheyev scored twice Thursday for the Lightning, doubling his season goal total in one night and twisting the dagger deeper into his former team.</p><h3><b>Physical presence</b></h3><p>The Hawks were credited with a season-high 31 hits. That was mostly thanks to their fourth line: Cole Smith, Ryan Greene and just-called-up Dillon Boucher. They combined for 16.</p><p>Smith said he's making a concerted effort to be more physical and believes "that's something, as a whole, we can increase."</p><p>Boucher also had a doozy of a fight against Lightning tough guy Jeff Viel. Blashill said Boucher has brought the exact elements to the lineup that he hoped to see.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="fr" dir="ltr">Boucher vs Viel HUGE TILT <a href="https://t.co/92b7tFimSO">pic.twitter.com/92b7tFimSO</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2118511837381525877?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 6, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Backing Blashill</b></h3><p>Connor Bedard raved about Blashill's coaching when asked about it Wednesday.</p><p>Of course, it's rare for any player to criticize his coach, so Bedard's words could taken with a grain of salt. But they seemed genuine, and they echoed the sentiments other players have recently vocalized.</p><p>"We love 'Blash,'" Bedard said. "We love how he approaches us, how he coaches our team. I know, on a personal note, how much better of a hockey player he's made me in the last year and a bit here. He's given us the right message, the right formula, and we've got to go execute better for 60 minutes.</p><p>"We're not focused on outside [noise]. ... We're focused on internal, and we feel like our whole coaching staff is doing a really good job. We want to go get some wins for them."</p><h3><b>Internal info</b></h3><p>Blashill's propensity to share some of the Hawks' internal analytics in interviews — particularly as evidence to support his claims that the team didn't actually play poorly in some recent losses — has backfired on him, becoming a running joke among hockey analytics-oriented commentators on social media.</p><p>Blashill admitted Wednesday it's unfair for him to consistently reference stats that reporters and the public don't have access to. He also shed light on where the organization's internal analytics come from.</p><p>"First off, we're doing our chances manually," Blashill said. "We have a criteria that we follow, and it's not favored towards us or towards the other team. I can say that because there's games where we've been out-chanced bad.</p><p>"There's a criteria that [video coach] Matt Meacham has gone through going back to his days with Joel Quenneville, so he's done it for a long time. We've tweaked the criteria a little bit based on further knowledge. It’s hard for anything that's automated to be as accurate as manual chances. You just can't do that across the league."</p>

entries.title: The 1-7 Bulls are a disaster, and that's putting it mildly
entries.summary: <p><i>“If the Bulls are awful and you don’t get the [Josh] Giddey answers you want . . . yeesh. They wouldn’t be in an impossible spot by any means, but you’d run the risk of prolonging the road to sustained success. Bulls fans deserve a lot better.” — Nekias Duncan, Yahoo Sports, October 20, 2026</i></p><p>‘Trash.”</p><p>Too harsh, right? Too soon, you think? The unfair but not necessarily wrong descriptive to use in describing the Bulls’ overall entrance into this season.</p><p>A 43-point loss. A 35-point loss. A 19-point second-half lead lost in a loss to the defending champs that made the incumbents feel like it was June and not October. And the next time they played the Knicks, just a week later, (in a game where Jalen Brunson outscored the entire Bulls team in the first quarter, his 22 to their 21) the Bulls gave up 84 points in the first half to go along with another 30-point loss to add to the list.</p><p>They had us at “Hello.”</p><p>To say the new, overhauled, new face-of-the-franchise, new front office, new coach and coaching staff Chicago Bulls squad’s introduction has been “less than” would be less than generous. The condemnation of a team and its season less than 10 games in has not yet arrived. But it is upon us.</p><p>As bad as things have been for the Bulls in recent decades it’s hard to say that they’ve had a start to a season like this one. Giving up 129.6 points per game through the first eight. Just a point over the 1990-91 Nuggets’ all-time record of 130.7. Not that that’s going to continue for the duration for the Bulls, but early, small-sampled, historical context matters, right? So if defense is the major key to winning a chip — then what is the end resulting assessment of anti-defense?</p><p>The mollywaps keep stacking. Questions keep piling. Uncertainty has their number.</p><p>Owners of the largest negative point differential in the League outside of Sacramento. It’s not that the Bulls don’t want or can’t play defense, they just haven’t learned how yet.<br>Collaboratively. And the singular, bigger problem they face other than that is that teams know, prepare and prey on that exact fact.</p><p>Next to last in field-goal percentage (41.2), dead last in three-point FG% (27.2). In the latest Knicks game they hit their first two threes of the game, then proceeded to miss their next 20 in a row — all in the first half. Putting up a total of 44 for the game. Making only 10. Who do they think they are: the 2024-25 Celtics? Somehow they’ve still found a way to lead the eague this season in free-throw attempts.</p><p>Which, of course, is on-brand negated by being 25th in the league in FT%. (Also 22nd in the league in turnovers and 28th in personal fouls, just to keep things 1,000%.</p><p>All of it is an unfair disadvantage that Tiago Splitter and Co. are going to have to figure out faster than immediately. Where even once they hit that 10-game threshold and they’re, say, 2-8, if they’ve found a way to drop that PPGA average to at or below 116, that would be miracle-ish.</p><p>Enough to make a blue state See Red.</p><p>This is the find out. What we asked for from ownership. New everything across the board. Since the trade-deadline fire sale last season, it seemed like every move they made was in the direction of making sure they were going to replicate the latest version of the other Reinsdorf-owned franchise across town. Not the basketball version of the previous three years of it.</p><p>Tryna put the pieces of them together, puzzling. Coaches, players. Players, players. No one really knows one another. Uncertainty is stalking. This early-season rush to the bottom is not the look this team wants to give out to be received as representative of who they are and destined to become.</p><p>Splitter is preaching resilience to Caleb Wilson. Acknowledging both his future star’s bad body language in games when they get behind by a lead that seems insurmountable and also keeping in mind that losing like this up until now, throughout the entire 20-years of his life, has been a totally unexperienced experience for the rookie. The same tempered level of grace and tough understanding the outside seems to be giving the team by taking all things unknown by them, about themselves, into perspective and consideration.</p><p>The work that needs to be done seems unconquerable. But not unattainable or an unreasonable ambition. Not yet, at least. Because breaking the generational cycle of losing they inherited won’t be easy to ghost or avoid. The bottom loves company and misery. Plus failure.</p><p>Organizational restructuring and accumulating young talent are less powerful in this particular instance than patience and prayer. Both allies for this team. If the Pope one Sunday shows up in Saint Peter’s Basilica for Mass wearing a Bulls cap, they might have a chance.</p><p>As long as they can evade the “trash” talk.</p><p>The bottom’s calling. Preying on ’em. And the Bulls aren’t really trying to swipe right.</p>

entries.title: No. 3 Illinois routs Penn in second game of year
entries.summary: <p>CHAMPAIGN — Andrej Stojavovic scored 25 points and Quentin Coleman had 19, including 15 in the second half, to lead No. 3 Illinois to a 112-70 victory Thursday over Penn.</p><p>Zavier Zens had 18 points, Ethan Brown had 13 points and 10 rebounds, Lincoln Williams had 12 points and nine rebounds in his collegiate debut and Stefan Vaaks tossed in 11 points for the Illini (2-0), who shot 59% from the field (43 of 73) and outrebounded Penn 62-33.</p><p>Illinois also scored in triple figures in its opener, beating Fairleigh Dickinson 120-45 on Monday.</p><p>Michael Zanoni scored 16 points for Penn (0-1) and Lucas Lueth had 14 points and three blocked shots.</p><p>Illinois led 53-30 at halftime. Stojakovic scored 21 points in the first half and Illinois outscored Penn 30-8 over the last 10:22 to break open a tight game.</p><p>The Illini played without returning starters David Mirkovic, an AP preseason All-American, and Jake Davis. Each is out indefinitely.</p><p>Mirkovic is recovering from foot surgery in August and an appendectomy Saturday. Davis suffered a separated shoulder early in the game vs. Fairleigh-Dickinson and underwent surgery Wednesday.</p><p>The Illini beat Penn 105-70 in a first-round NCAA Tournament game last season with Mirkovic scoring 29 points and collecting 17 rebounds and went on to play in the Final Four.</p><p>Ivy League preseason favorite Penn has four returning starters and seven of its top nine scorers back from last year's team, which won the league tournament and earned its first NCAA Tournament berth since 2018.</p><p>Ex-Iowa coach Fran McCaffery is in his second year as the Quakers’ coach. Illinois was 16-11 against McCaffery in his 15 years in charge of the Hawkeyes.</p><p>Up next: Penn: Hosts Howard on Monday; Illinois: At No. 19 Texas Tech on Tuesday.</p><p></p><p><b>Loyola 76, West Georgia 53</b></p><p>Dayan Nessah had 15 points in Loyola’s 76-53 victory against West Georgia at Gentile Arena.</p><p>Nessah also added five rebounds for the Ramblers (2-0). Jason Schofield scored 12 points while finishing 6 of 7 from the floor, and added six rebounds. Jayden Dawson had 12 points and shot 4 for 8, including 3 for 7 from beyond the arc.</p><p>Lou Hutchinson finished with 16 points for the Wolves (0-2). Kenneth Chime added 14 points and six rebounds for West Georgia. Chas Lewless also had eight points.</p><p>Loyola Chicago took the lead with 19:22 remaining in the first half and did not trail again. Schofield led their team in scoring with 12 points in the first half to help put them up 42-29 at the break. Loyola Chicago extended its lead to 49-29 during the second half, fueled by a 7-0 scoring run. Guillaume Grotzinger scored a team-high seven points in the second half as their team closed out the win.</p><p>Up next: Both teams next play Wednesday. Loyola Chicago visits Air Force and West Georgia plays UNC Asheville at home.</p>

entries.title: 'This cannot be real,' says neighbor who heard screams of 4 family members killed in Rogers Park blaze
entries.summary: <p>A fire tore through a Rogers Park townhome early Thursday morning, killing a family of four, including a 13-year-old boy and their dog, police, witnesses and an alderperson said. </p><p>The 13-year-old boy was identified as Kilmer International Academy eighth grader Valentino Vallejo in an email to school families from Kilmer Principal Natalie Rodriguez.</p><p>Rodriguez said the school will have grief counseling and other support available for students and provide funeral information when it's available.</p><p>"We are devastated by news of a tragic house fire this morning in our community and the loss of one of our CPS 8th graders and members of their family," the statement said. "Our thoughts are first and foremost with this student’s family members, loved ones, and the school community."</p><p>Two women, 69 and 46, and a 22-year-old man were also found unresponsive at the two-story home around 4:15 a.m., Chicago police said.</p><p>They were taken to area hospitals where they were pronounced dead, police said.</p><p>Their names were not being released immediately, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office.</p><p>Angelita Sanchez organized a <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/help-our-family-lay-our-loved-ones-to-rest" target="_blank" >GoFundMe page</a> to help with funeral expenses. The victims were her mother, sister and two nephews.</p><p>"There are simply no words to describe the heartbreak of losing not one, but four people we love so deeply, all at once," the fundraiser description reads. "Our hearts are shattered, and we are facing a reality we never could have prepared for."</p><p>Elise Adu, who lives two units down from where the fire started at 7049 N. Paulina St., woke up to her neighbors screaming out their window for help. One of the family members, she said, shouted that they “didn’t have their phone.”</p><p>She remembered thinking, "This cannot be real."</p><p>“I grabbed my phone and ran to my parents’ room and said, 'Something’s happening outside, we need to call 911,'" Adu, 27, said. </p><p>After she, her parents and their dog got outside, she set out to wake the neighbors. And an awful thought dawned on her.</p><p>“I kept thinking that if someone’s inside, they’re not surviving that,” she said.</p><p>Adu saw the family — a grandmother, mother and two grandchildren — every day. She'd often leave her keys with them while on family trips.</p><p>"It's a horrific tragedy to lose an entire family,'' 49th Ward Ald. Maria Hadden told the Chicago Sun-Times. “They had a dog they walked, and a lot of people knew them. They were a lovely family. It hits really hard.” </p><p>Hadden confirmed the GoFundMe, which had raised more than $22,000 as of 7:40 p.m. Thursday and was increasing by the minute, was organized by the family of the victims.</p><p>Hadden confirmed the dog, which Adu said was a brown 4-year-old Labradoodle named Remi, died in the fire. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item">
